key_concept: Only an organic compound containing sulphur gives a positive sulphur test on its sodium fusion extract (Lassaigne's extract), so the answer must be the sulphur-containing amino acid.
steps: During sodium fusion, sulphur in the compound becomes sodium sulphide: $2Na + S \rightarrow Na_2S$.
If nitrogen is also present, sodium thiocyanate forms as well: $Na + C + N + S \rightarrow NaSCN$.
With sodium nitroprusside, sulphide gives a violet/purple complex: $S^{2-} + [Fe(CN)_5NO]^{2-} \rightarrow [Fe(CN)_5NOS]^{4-}$.
With $FeCl_3$, thiocyanate gives the blood-red colour: $Fe^{3+} + SCN^- \rightarrow [Fe(SCN)]^{2+}$.
Whichever of these colours is meant, the compound must contain sulphur.
Leucine ($C_6H_{13}NO_2$), threonine ($C_4H_9NO_3$) and serine ($C_3H_7NO_3$) contain no sulphur.
Methionine, $CH_3SCH_2CH_2CH(NH_2)COOH$, contains sulphur (and nitrogen), so it is the answer.
why_not_others: Threonine and serine carry $-OH$ groups and leucine is a plain alkyl amino acid. None of them contains sulphur, so their extracts give no sulphur test.
common_trap: Students mix up the colour–reagent pairs: nitroprusside with $S^{2-}$ gives violet, while blood-red comes from $Fe^{3+}$ with $SCN^-$ (both N and S present).
time_saving_tip: Any sulphur-test question on amino acids reduces to spotting the sulphur-containing one, either methionine or cysteine.
key_check_note: The question pairs the wrong colour with the reagent. Nitroprusside gives a violet colour with sulphide; blood-red is the $FeCl_3$/thiocyanate test. Both tests point only to methionine, so the key (3) stands.
